children: By Karen Hube

At a time when some of the wealthiest Americans use strategies to drop into low tax brackets and pay no federal income taxes in some years, many folks may wonder: Is it possible to achieve this themselves?
With careful planning, it may be.

Taxpayers have more flexibility to drive down their tax rates than they may think, and it has become even easier thanks to juicier tax deductions ushered in by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) passed last year.

"I call it taking a tax holiday," says Erin Scannell, CEO of Ameriprise's Heritage Wealth Advisors. "It opens up the tax playbook dramatically. People save not just in the year they get their tax rates down, but over their lifetimes because a tax holiday enables strategies that set you up for future tax savings."

The planning involves a three-phase process: reducing taxable income for a tax year; arranging for enough liquidity to support your lifestyle in your low-income year; and putting strategies to work for long-term benefits.
Qualifying for a Lower Rate — Perhaps Even a 0% Rate

The lowest income-tax rate is 10%, applied to taxable income of up to $24,800 for couples filing jointly and $12,400 for singles, but the standard deduction or itemized deductions can offset income and create an effective 0% rate.

To qualify for a 0% capital-gains tax rate, taxable income must be no more than $98,900 for couples filing jointly and $49,450 for single filers. Income over those thresholds falls in the 15% capital gains bracket, and over $613,700 and $545,500 respectively in the 20% bracket.

Remember these thresholds for taxable income, not gross income, says Sherman Standberry, founder and CEO of My CPA Coach. "People with salaries well over $100,000 may not realize they're in range of the 0% capital-gains tax bracket."
A married couple earning $130,000 may assume the 0% bracket is out of reach, but after claiming the 2026 standard deduction of $32,200 for couples filing taxes jointly, they would be eligible.

For taxpayers with high incomes, the standard deduction won't lower taxable incomes enough to qualify for a 0% tax, so they have two options: "Defer income into another year or use deductions to offset your income," Scannell says.
Self-employed or newly retired people have an easier time driving down tax rates because they may have more control over when and how they draw taxable income.

A contractor might defer invoicing into a subsequent year. A retiree who hasn't yet started Social Security or required minimum distributions (RMDs) from deferred retirement accounts can postpone realizing gains and rejigger asset location, so income-producing investments are in tax-deferred accounts.
It can be more challenging for people with regular income, such as payrolled workers, retirees taking RMDs, or investment property owners receiving monthly rent.

"But don't let perfection be the enemy of good planning," says Greg Welborn, principal at First Financial Consulting. "Focus on minimizing taxes. A 0% capital gains rate is great, but don't forget that 15% is better than 20%."
There is a long menu of income-reducing strategies, some of which were enhanced by the OBBBA.
Taxpayers can max out pretax contributions to retirement accounts and health savings accounts (HSAs), and bunch future years' charitable contributions to score a fat deduction.

Those who own a business or rental property can purchase deductible equipment or improvements. Under the OBBBA you can immediately write off 100% of certain costs rather than the 20% originally set for this year.

Seniors may qualify for further deductions such as the OBBBA's new $6,000 deduction for taxpayers 65 and older. This tax break phases out once income reaches $250,000 for joint filers and $175,000 for singles.
Creating Liquidity to Live On
Building a stash of liquidity to live on during a tax holiday may require planning a year or more in advance.
Investors can tap cash-equivalent investments and consider selling stock shares with no or very little appreciation, Scannell says.
Consider a loan. "Some people hate the idea of going into debt for their tax holiday, but when you compare the interest you pay and the tax savings, this often makes sense," Scannell says.

If your living expenses are $100,000 and you borrow that at, say, a 6% rate, that is a $6,000 cost. "But if you took that $100,000 out of your investments you might end up paying a lot more in taxes," Scannell says.
Strategies With Long-Term Tax Benefits
In a 0% capital-gains tax year, selling appreciated stock to diversify or rebalance your portfolio is a priority.
You could even sell and immediately rebuy appreciated investments to give yourself a free step-up in cost basis, says Brian Schultz, a tax partner at Plante Moran.

Wash sale rules require 30 days before and after selling a losing investment before buying it back if you want to use the loss to offset gains. "But there are no equivalent wash-sale rules for gains," Schultz says.
Another move with long-term tax benefits: Convert assets in a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA, which allows future tax-free withdrawals and has no RMDs.
Converted assets are subject to income-tax rates. In a year with an inordinately low or zero effective tax rate, you snag a discount on the tax cost of your conversion.
